primary_source: Pamuk (2009) 'Estimating GDP per capita for the Ottoman Empire in a European Comparative Framework 1500-1820' XVth World Economic History Congress Utrecht
methodology_notes: Backward extrapolation from 1500 benchmark using urbanization and wage data; ~27% total growth 1500-1820 implies ~0.08% p.a. Rise phase likely slightly higher due to territorial expansion
limitations: No direct GDP data exists; all estimates indirect via wages/urbanization; territorial expansion conflates per-capita vs aggregate growth

primary_source: Pamuk (2009) 'Estimating GDP per capita for the Ottoman Empire' Utrecht
methodology_notes: Stagnation to mild growth; Ottoman Empire at relative height in Mediterranean in 16th century then relative decline like Italy and Spain; growth rate below 0.4% consistent with Southern European peers
limitations: Per capita vs aggregate ambiguity; regional diversity not captured; few benchmark years available

primary_source: Pamuk (2009); Maddison Project Database
methodology_notes: Mild growth or stagnation; if 1820 GDP/cap ~$600 (1990 intl $) and 1500 ~$600 then ~27% growth over 320 years distributed unevenly; decline phase shows deceleration
limitations: Territorial losses complicate aggregate vs per-capita distinction; regional variation enormous

primary_source: Pamuk (2006) 'Estimating Economic Growth in the Middle East since 1820' JEH vol.66 no.3 pp.809-828
methodology_notes: 0.56% average for 1820-1913; includes negative shock of -4% during 1870-1880 decade; second-generation estimates suggest relatively higher GDP than first-generation
limitations: More data available for 19th century but still limited; 1870-1880 shock from Russo-Turkish War and fiscal crisis

primary_source: Karaman & Pamuk (2010) 'Ottoman State Finances in European Perspective 1500-1914' JEH vol.70 no.3 pp.593-629
methodology_notes: Central treasury cash revenues below 4% of GDP during early modern era; comparable to large European states in 16th century; per capita revenue < 3 days wages of unskilled Istanbul worker
limitations: Measures central treasury cash only; excludes timar/in-kind revenues which were substantial; actual extraction from taxpayers unknown

primary_source: Barkan 'Bir Butce Ornegi' pp.251-329; cited in Karaman & Pamuk (2010)
methodology_notes: Ex-post budget document from Ottoman archives; ~9.65 million Venetian ducats; comparable to all European states except France and Spain
limitations: Single year snapshot; central treasury only; excludes provincial retention

primary_source: Karaman & Pamuk (2010) JEH
secondary_source: Over 40 budget documents compiled from Ottoman archives
methodology_notes: Central treasury collections; 1527 data shows central treasury collected 46% of assessed revenues; high intermediary shares reduced effective centralization
limitations: Tax farming (iltizam) system means large gap between assessed and centrally collected; actual burden higher

primary_source: Karaman & Pamuk (2010) JEH
methodology_notes: Central treasury share fell to ~25% of collections by 18th century; malikane system (1695) privatized revenue streams; intermediaries captured growing share
limitations: Malikane holders retained large portions; effective state capacity declining even as nominal GDP may have grown

primary_source: Karaman & Pamuk (2010) JEH; Tanzimat reform data
secondary_source: Pamuk 'Evolution of Fiscal Institutions' LSE working paper
methodology_notes: Significant fiscal centralization in 19th century responding to military defeats; revenue increases but still lagging European peers
limitations: OPDA captured portion of revenues; wartime/reform distortions; GDP denominator uncertain

primary_source: Pamuk (2000) A Monetary History of the Ottoman Empire CUP
methodology_notes: No external borrowing; fiscal deficits managed through debasement and internal mechanisms; timar system provided military service without cash expenditure
limitations: Absence of formal debt does not mean absence of fiscal stress; debasement served as implicit taxation

primary_source: Pamuk (2000) CUP; Salzmann (1993)
secondary_source: Balla & Johnson fiscal crisis comparison paper
methodology_notes: No external debt; internal borrowing from Galata bankers and sarrafs for short-term needs; esham system not yet introduced (comes 1775)
limitations: Informal obligations to Galata bankers not well documented; military arrears could constitute implicit debt

primary_source: Salzmann (1993) 'Ancien Regime Revisited' Politics & Society 21(4):393-423
methodology_notes: Esham bonds introduced 1775 as life annuities against future tax revenues; first formal domestic borrowing instrument; amount modest initially
limitations: No GDP denominator available; esham volume estimates vary; life-annuity structure makes valuation complex

primary_source: Ottoman public debt records; first loan £3M at 6% interest issued at 80%
secondary_source: Birdal (2010) Political Economy of Ottoman Public Debt
methodology_notes: First foreign loan 1854 for Crimean War; £3M nominal yielding ~£2.4M net; pre-war budget ~7.5M Ottoman liras
limitations: GDP estimate extremely uncertain for 1854; ratio is rough approximation

primary_source: Ottoman public debt records; Birdal (2010); Reinhart & Rogoff dataset
methodology_notes: Nominal debt £200-214.5M; annual debt service £12M = 50%+ of revenue; 15 loans struck 1854-1874; net receipts only ~46% of nominal due to deep discounts
limitations: GDP not known precisely; ratio extrapolated from debt/revenue ratio of >50% and revenue/GDP ratio of ~5-10%; actual debt/GDP could be 75-200%

primary_source: Decree of Muharrem 1881; debt reduced from £252.8M to £106.4M
methodology_notes: Post-restructuring; OPDA controlled ~32-40% of state revenues for debt service; total includes arrears reduction
limitations: Post-haircut figure; effective burden still enormous; GDP denominator uncertain

primary_source: Ottoman debt records £139.1M Turkish pounds; Paris Conference 1925 records
methodology_notes: Debt £139.1M at 1914; new borrowing post-1882 under OPDA oversight; debt service manageable due to OPDA efficiency but sovereignty cost enormous
limitations: Pre-WWI figure; wartime debt excluded; GDP estimate for 1913 uncertain

primary_source: Pamuk (2000) A Monetary History of the Ottoman Empire CUP
secondary_source: Inalcik (1994) Ottoman economic and social history
methodology_notes: No formal government borrowing; fiscal needs met through timar system and debasement seigniorage
limitations: Absence of borrowing means absence of rate data; implicit cost of debasement not captured

primary_source: Pamuk (2000) CUP
methodology_notes: Short-term borrowing from Galata sarrafs at unknown but likely high rates; no formal bond market
limitations: Informal sarraf lending rates not systematically recorded

primary_source: Salzmann (1993); esham-i cedid 1871 at 10%
methodology_notes: Esham life annuities implied return ~10%; 1840 kaime paper currency issued at 12.5% interest functioning as bond
limitations: Esham returns hard to compute precisely due to life-annuity structure; limited secondary market

primary_source: Ottoman loan records 1854; £3M at 6% issued at 80%
secondary_source: Birdal (2010) Political Economy of Ottoman Public Debt
methodology_notes: First foreign loan; 6% coupon but issued at 80% of par giving effective yield ~7.5%; guaranteed by Egyptian tribute
limitations: Well-documented first sovereign bond; effective rate higher than nominal due to discount

primary_source: Ottoman loan records; UK/France guaranteed
methodology_notes: UK/France guarantee during Crimean War reduced rate to 4%; issued at 102.6% of par (premium)
limitations: Exceptional rate due to great-power guarantee; not representative of Ottoman credit standing

primary_source: Ottoman loan records; 15 loans 1854-1874
secondary_source: Pamuk (2000); Homer & Sylla (2005) History of Interest Rates 4th ed.
methodology_notes: Nominal coupons 5-9% but deep discounts (1870 lottery loan at 32% of par = 3% coupon but ~9% effective; 1874 loan at 43.5% of par = 5% coupon but ~11.5% effective); deteriorating credit
limitations: Effective rates vary dramatically by calculation method; commissions and fees add further costs

primary_source: Contemporary records; Galata bankers refused to lend at 25%
secondary_source: Cited in multiple Ottoman debt studies
methodology_notes: Galata bankers refused to lend to government even at 25% interest in 1874 indicating total credit collapse
limitations: Anecdotal but well-attested; represents credit market failure not equilibrium rate

primary_source: Ramazan Kararnamesi October 1875
methodology_notes: Post-default: government proposed 5% bonds with 10-year maturity for creditors; effectively a forced restructuring
limitations: Not a market rate; imposed unilaterally during sovereign default

primary_source: OPDA records; risk premium fell from 5.7% to 2.1%
methodology_notes: Post-OPDA renewed access to European capital markets; risk premium compression from 5.7% to 2.1% reflects credibility of foreign fiscal control
limitations: Rate improvement came at cost of sovereignty; OPDA controlled 32-40% of revenues

primary_source: Kuran (2011) The Long Divergence; general Ottoman credit market literature
methodology_notes: Limited formal credit markets; sarraf money-changers and informal lending; Islamic usury prohibition nominally in effect but circumvented
limitations: Very sparse data for this period; rates inferred from later evidence and comparable economies

primary_source: Kuran & Rubin (2018) 'Financial Power of the Powerless' Economic Journal 128:758-96
secondary_source: Korkut & Bulut 'Ottoman Cash Waqfs: An Alternative Financial System' Insight Turkey
methodology_notes: Cash waqfs charged 10-15% with 15% legal cap per Ebussuud decree; rates disguised through legal ruses (istighlal); lenders charged privileged groups MORE (Muslims +1.9% vs non-Muslims)
limitations: Cash waqf rates represent regulated segment; unregulated market rates likely higher; Kuran-Rubin data from Istanbul 1602-1799

primary_source: Kuran & Rubin (2018) Economic Journal 128:758-96; dataset of private loans Istanbul 1602-1799
methodology_notes: Male Muslim elites paid ~19-20%; men paid 3.4% more than women; Muslims 1.9% more than non-Muslims; elites 2.3% more; paradoxical premium due to judicial favoritism creating moral hazard
limitations: Istanbul-specific; court-registered loans only; informal market not captured; selection bias toward documented transactions

primary_source: Kuran & Rubin (2018); Damascus creditor records at 24%
methodology_notes: Widening range as formal institutions weakened; Damascus reports 24%; Galata banker rates for merchants lower at 12-18%; cash waqf rates stable at 10-15%
limitations: Regional variation enormous; Damascus ≠ Istanbul; wartime vs peacetime rates diverge

primary_source: Ottoman Bank records; Galata banker lending rates
methodology_notes: Ottoman Bank (1856/1863) and Galata banker network provided commercial credit; rates declined as formal banking expanded; still higher than Western European peers
limitations: Foreign-owned banks served different clientele than traditional sarrafs; dual credit market

primary_source: Inalcik (1994) An Economic and Social History of the Ottoman Empire CUP
secondary_source: Pamuk (1987) Ottoman Empire and European Capitalism
methodology_notes: Transit trade revenues substantial; control of Silk Road termini; Constantinople 1453 capture redirected trade flows; no systematic trade statistics exist
limitations: No quantitative trade data available for this period; inference from narrative sources only

primary_source: Inalcik (1994); Pamuk (1987)
secondary_source: Lampe; McGowan cited in economic history of Ottoman Empire
methodology_notes: Capitulations 1536 granted France low duties (3% import/export); Balkans ran export surplus; Constantinople ran import surplus; empire overall roughly balanced
limitations: Capitulations regime complicates analysis; re-export trade significant; no consolidated trade statistics

primary_source: Lampe; McGowan; Pamuk (1987) Ottoman Empire and European Capitalism
methodology_notes: Cotton exports doubled 1750-1789; Balkans maintained export surplus; overall empire shifting as European manufactures penetrate; 3% capitulation tariffs prevented protection
limitations: Transition period poorly documented; regional variation extreme; re-exports and transit trade complicate

primary_source: Pamuk (1987) Ottoman Empire and European Capitalism CUP; Quataert in Inalcik & Quataert (1994)
methodology_notes: 1838 Treaty of Balta Liman opened markets; imports grew ~8x vs exports ~4x; deindustrialization; by 1900 UK/France/Germany/Austria = 75% of imports 60-70% of exports; trade deficit chronic
limitations: Exact figures disputed; Quataert argues handicrafts resisted better than assumed; Great Depression of 1873-96 temporarily aided import-competing sectors

primary_source: Pamuk (2000) A Monetary History of the Ottoman Empire CUP Table 3.1 Graph A-2
secondary_source: Akce Wikipedia/Grokipedia summary of Pamuk data
methodology_notes: Silver content stable at 1.15-1.20g; very minor fluctuations; period of monetary stability
limitations: Limited numismatic evidence for earliest period; stability well-established by scholarly consensus

primary_source: Pamuk (2000) CUP; Mehmed II debasement episodes
methodology_notes: 30% total reduction over ~4 decades under Mehmed II; debasements roughly every 10 years; silver fell from ~1.15g to ~0.77g
limitations: Well-documented period; Bayezid II reversed policy after 1481

primary_source: Pamuk (2000) CUP
methodology_notes: Bayezid II ended periodic debasements; silver content ~0.73-0.77g; monetary stability restored
limitations: Short period but well-documented; stability confirmed by numismatic evidence

primary_source: Pamuk (2000) CUP; Pamuk (2004) 'Prices in the Ottoman Empire 1469-1914'
methodology_notes: Silver content declined at 0.52% annual rate 1469-1585; two debasements (1489 and 1566); content fell ~12% from ~0.7g to ~0.68g over 96 years
limitations: Gradual decline; Pamuk argues debasement more important than silver inflows for price increases

primary_source: Pamuk (2000) CUP; 'Great Debasement of 1585-86'
secondary_source: Pamuk (2001) 'Price Revolution in the Ottoman Empire Reconsidered' IJMES 33
methodology_notes: Catastrophic: 44% reduction in single episode 1585-86 (0.68g to 0.38g); further to 0.29g by 1600; triggered by fiscal crisis of Long War
limitations: Well-documented monetary crisis; Janissary revolts linked to debasement

primary_source: Pamuk (2000) CUP; silver content 0.29g (1600) to 0.13g (1700)
secondary_source: Pamuk (1997) 'In the Absence of Domestic Currency' JEH 57
methodology_notes: From 0.29g to 0.13g; includes period of akce cessation mid-17th century; debased European coinage circulated widely; kurus introduced as replacement
limitations: Complex period; akce partially replaced; calculation complicated by currency substitution

primary_source: Pamuk (2000) CUP; silver content 0.13g (1700) to 0.048g (1800)
methodology_notes: Continued decline; kurus became primary unit (fixed at 120 akce); early kurus ~20g at 60% silver also debased
limitations: Akce becoming vestigial unit; kurus debasement is more relevant metric for this period

primary_source: Pamuk (2000) CUP; 'Great Debasement of Mahmud II'
methodology_notes: Most rapid debasement: 0.048g (1800) to 0.032g (1810s) to 0.008g (1840s); Mahmud II fiscal desperation; kaime paper currency introduced 1840 at 12.5% interest
limitations: Terminal phase of akce; effectively worthless; replaced by kurus and paper currency

primary_source: Kuran (2011) The Long Divergence; Pamuk (2000) CUP
methodology_notes: Sarraf money-changers only; no formal banking; Islamic prohibition on interest nominally enforced; waqf system provided some credit functions but not banking per se
limitations: Scale assessment based on comparative institutional analysis; no formal banking institutions

primary_source: Kuran & Rubin (2018); Korkut & Bulut on cash waqfs
methodology_notes: Cash waqfs emerged as proto-banking (10-15% lending); Galata sarrafs provided exchange and short-term credit; no joint-stock banking; no central bank; Kuran: no 'durable financial institutions recognizable as banks' before 19th century
limitations: Cash waqfs innovative but limited in scale; sarraf network informal; no deposit-taking institutions proper

primary_source: Kuran (2011); Salzmann (1993); esham system 1775
methodology_notes: Galata bankers (Armenian/Greek/Jewish) increasingly important; esham bonds 1775 = proto-government bond market; sarraf/banker network handles state borrowing; but no chartered banks
limitations: Galata bankers sophisticated but not institutionalized; family-based; no limited liability; no branching

primary_source: Ottoman Bank Wikipedia/Grokipedia; Hosgor 'Credit and Financing in Early Modern Ottoman Empire'
secondary_source: Daily Sabah Ottoman banking history series
methodology_notes: Bank-i Dersaadet 1847 (failed quickly); Banque de Constantinople 1847-1852 (wound up); kaime paper currency 1840; Ottoman Bank 1856 (British); Imperial Ottoman Bank 1863 (Anglo-French) with note-issuing privilege
limitations: Rapid institutionalization but all foreign-owned/controlled; domestic banking capacity nil

primary_source: Ottoman Bank records; OPDA records; Pamuk fiscal history
methodology_notes: Imperial Ottoman Bank as de facto central bank; multiple foreign banks; Galata bankers still active; OPDA as parallel fiscal institution; but banking remained dominated by foreign capital and non-Muslim minorities
limitations: Banking development real but exogenous; no domestically-owned major bank; serves foreign trade/debt interests primarily

primary_source: Kuran (2011) The Long Divergence
methodology_notes: No formal capital markets; no tradeable securities; no secondary market for any financial instrument; land/tax assignments (timar) not tradeable
limitations: Absence well-documented; no institutional basis for capital markets

primary_source: Kuran (2011); Salzmann (1993)
methodology_notes: Malikane (life-term tax farms from 1695 = late peak/early decline) somewhat tradeable; cash waqf shares had limited transferability; no organized exchange; iltizam contracts auctioned but not secondary-traded
limitations: Malikane introduction in 1695 is borderline peak/decline; no formal market infrastructure

primary_source: Salzmann (1993); esham bond records; EHES working paper 112
methodology_notes: Esham bonds (1775) = first tradeable government debt; traded informally among Galata bankers; no organized exchange yet; malikane and esham created embryonic secondary market
limitations: Limited liquidity; no price transparency; restricted to elite investor class in Istanbul

primary_source: Borsa Istanbul historical records; Dersaadet Tahvilat Borsasi records
secondary_source: EHES WP 112 'Evidence from the Ottoman Empire and the Istanbul Bourse'
methodology_notes: Dersaadet Tahvilat Borsasi (Istanbul Bond Exchange) established 1866; formalized 1873; traded government bonds (esham/tahvilat); commercial code 1861 enabled joint-stock companies; 20 Greek members on exchange committee; expanded to stocks and FX by 1906
limitations: Exchange real but narrow; dominated by government debt; limited equity market; foreign-controlled; 1873 Vienna crisis disrupted early operations
